deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft of Riemann's 1851 Inaugural-Dissertation, around Art. 18–21. The previous page proves the Riemann mapping theorem. A simply connected, bounded, possibly branched surface T over the z-plane is mapped by w = e^t conformally onto a surface S lying once over the unit disk K. The present page studies the derivative of that map. Its goal is a relation between the total turning of the boundary of T and the total branching of T.

(1) Local behaviour. At an ordinary point of T, dw/dz is finite and nonzero; this was shown at the end of the previous page via Art. 12, using that z(w) is single-valued on the unbranched S.
Now take a branch point O' of order n−1 over z = z'. Set t = (z−z')^{1/n}. By Art. 14, w is a single-valued continuous (analytic) function of t, and dw/dt is finite and nonzero; nonzero because the map is one-to-one (my gloss).
Hence dw/dz = (dw/dt)·(1/n)·t^{1−n}.
So log(dw/dz) − (1/n − 1)·log(z−z') stays finite at O'.

(2) Harmonic function. Put log(dw/dz) = u + v i. Then u is harmonic on T except at the branch points. Near O', writing z − z' = ρ e^{iφ}, the difference u − (1/n−1) log ρ tends to a finite limit.

(3) Flux by Green (Art. 9, III). The flux ∫ ∂u/∂p ds over the whole boundary of T (p the inner normal) equals the sum of the fluxes over arbitrarily small curves enclosing the branch points.
Around a single O' the corrected function u − (1/n−1) log ρ is regular, so its flux vanishes:
∫ ∂u/∂p ds − (1/n−1) ∫ ∂(log ρ)/∂p ds = 0.
On the image this is written as + ((n−1)/n)·∫…, which is the same thing.
Take as the curve a circle about O'. Over the branch point it closes only after n turns, so φ runs from 0 to 2nπ and ds = ρ dφ. The normal points toward O', so ∂/∂p = −∂/∂ρ. Then
∫ ∂u/∂p ds = −(1/n−1)·∫_0^{2nπ} (∂ log ρ/∂ρ)·ρ dφ = −(1/n−1)·2nπ = 2π(n−1).
Summing over all branch points, the flux over the boundary of T (or over any part of T containing all branch points) is
2π·Σ(n−1) = 2πV,
where V is the sum of the orders of the branch points.

(4) Geometric evaluation on the boundary.
- Let ds be a boundary element of T with tangent angle φ, and dσ the corresponding element on the boundary of S with tangent angle ψ.
- Then dz = ds·e^{φi} and dw = dσ·e^{ψi}.
- So on the boundary log(dw/dz) = log(dσ/ds) + (ψ − φ) i, i.e. v = ψ − φ.
- By Cauchy–Riemann, ∂u/∂p = −∂v/∂s; this is the same relation as ∂n/∂s = −∂m/∂p on the previous page.
- Hence ∫ ∂u/∂p ds along any arc equals −Δv = Δφ − Δψ. Corner points where ∂u/∂p is infinite are handled by a limit over a small rounding arc.
- On the full positively oriented boundary, Δψ = 2π, since ∂S runs once around the circle. Write Δφ = 2πK, where K is the total turning ("ganze Krümmung") of ∂T.
- So the flux is 2π(K − 1).

(5) Comparing the two evaluations gives K − 1 = V. The total turning number of the boundary of a simply connected branched planar domain equals 1 plus the total branching order. This is a turning-number (Umlaufsatz) / Riemann–Hurwitz-type relation, proved through the conformal map onto the disk.
errors: Sign conventions are implicit. The identity at the branch point is correct, ∫∂u/∂p ds − (1/n−1)∫∂logρ/∂p ds = 0; the image reads '+ (n−1)/n', which is equivalent. The next step then replaces ∂/∂p by −∂/∂ρ without saying so, which is valid only with the normal pointing toward O'. The final value 2π(n−1) is correct, as the check with w = z^{1/2} confirms.

In Green's theorem (Art. 9, III) as stated with inner normals, the boundary flux equals the flux over the small curves only if those curves carry normals pointing into the small neighbourhoods. This is consistent with step (3) but not stated.
The nonvanishing of dw/dt at a branch point is used tacitly; it follows from the injectivity of the map onto S. This is not argued on this page beyond the reference to Art. 14.

The transcription has the total turning attributed to 'Begrenzung von S'. Logically it must be the boundary of T (∂S, a circle, has turning 1), and the image appears to read T. If S was written, it is a slip.
The treatment of boundary corners, where ∂u/∂p becomes infinite, is only sketched ('selbstredend der Grenzwerth…').

results.what: At a branch point of order n−1 of the bordered surface T, log(dw/dz) − (1/n − 1)·log(z − z') is finite for the Riemann mapping function w.
results.modern_name: Local normal form of a conformal map at a branch point (uniformizing parameter t = (z−z')^{1/n})

results.what: The flux of u = log|w'| around a branch point of order n−1 is 2π(n−1); the total boundary flux is 2πV.
results.modern_name: Argument principle / Gauss–Green flux computation for log|f'|
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (argument principle); Riemann for the Green's-theorem version on branched surfaces

results.what: For a simply connected branched surface T conformally equivalent to the disk, the total turning K of its boundary satisfies K − 1 = V, the sum of the branch orders.
results.modern_name: Turning-number theorem (Hopf Umlaufsatz) for branched immersed disks; a bordered Riemann–Hurwitz / Gauss–Bonnet-type relation
results.usually_credited_to: H. Hopf (Umlaufsatz, 1935); Riemann–Hurwitz (Hurwitz 1891) for branching counts

deep.surprise_reason: The local analysis and the flux computation are standard dissertation-era Riemann. The explicit relation 'total boundary curvature − 1 = total branch order' for a simply connected branched surface is a neat early form of the Umlaufsatz / Riemann–Hurwitz relation for bordered surfaces. I am not sure it appears in this form in the published dissertation, so it is a notable but modest unpublished detail. It flows naturally from his methods and the result is easy.

checkable.asserts: The flux of log ρ over a circle traversed n times equals 2nπ.
Example w = z^(1/2) on the 2-sheeted unit disk (n=2): the boundary flux of u = log|dw/dz| with inner normal is 2π = 2π(K−1) with K=2, and also 2πV with V=1.
d/dz (z−z')^{1/n} = (1/n)(z−z')^{1/n−1}, so log(dw/dz) − (1/n−1)log(z−z') is finite; expected output 1/n.

transcription_corrections: In the equation for the circle around O', the image appears to read '+ ((n−1)/n) ∫ ∂logρ/∂p ds = 0', not '+ (1/n − 1)'. With (n−1)/n the identity is correct.
'Begrenzung von S = K 2π' should probably read 'Begrenzung von T'; the image seems to show T.
'x und u[?]-Axe': uncertain; probably the axis of the second plane ('x- und u-Axe', or the real axis of w). The angles φ, ψ are tangent angles in the z- and w-planes respectively.
'Bordes[?]' is likely 'Bogens' or 'Kreises' (an infinitely close rounding arc).
First line: 'aber dw/d(z−z')^{1/n}' is followed by an implied 'einen endlichen Werth hat, da …'.
'in Bezug auf beliebig [enge→] kleine Umgrenzungen': the image shows a correction above the line; reading 'kleine' is plausible.
